I'm testing a pattern: within each contiguous run of 0s and 3s in a row, the 3 shifts to the leftmost position of that run. It checks out on the first two rows of example1, but a query case seems to break the rule since the 3 was already leftmost yet the output still changes.

Reconsidering, I try alternative rules — maybe the 3 slides left off the grid edge when nothing blocks it, or maybe it actually moves rightward, jumping over 8s to land in the next open run.

Counting the 3s across rows shows the totals don't match: five in the input but only four in the output, so one 3 seems to vanish somewhere in the transformation.

Mapping the output 3 positions against the input 3 positions, it looks like each 3 shifted to a new location, so I'm testing whether they moved one step earlier in the reading-order sequence of non-8 cells - flattening the grid's 0/3 cells and shifting each 3 backward by one position in that sequence.

That doesn't line up with the actual output though, so I'm trying another idea: maybe each 3 slides to the left end of its contiguous run of non-8 cells within its row, or possibly wraps around within that run instead of just moving to the edge.

But r0's isolated 3 at col0 disappears while r3's isolated 3 at col0 jumps to col2, so the rule isn't simply "move to start of run" — I'm trying to reconcile these two cases, maybe the 3 jumps over the blocking 8 to land right after it, but r0 has no landing spot so it vanishes instead.

Testing that vanish rule against row1 of query3 breaks it though—3 at col1 with left-end col0 should give col0, but actual output shows 3 at col3, so that theory fails too. I'm now wondering if this is actually a column-wise shift rather than row-wise.

Comparing input and output 3 positions across rows: (1,1)→(2,1) drops down one row, while (2,3)→(1,3) moves up one row, so maybe each 3 moves vertically depending on something about its run, not horizontally as I assumed.

Testing "shift up by one" across other cells: (0,0)'s 3 shifts up and vanishes off-grid, (3,0)'s 3 shifts down to r4 correctly. But checking (4,4), that column has no 3 in the output at all — the 3 seems to disappear entirely rather than following the same shift rule.

The direction of movement doesn't seem consistent per 3 — (1,1) moves down, (2,3) moves up, (3,0) moves down, others vanish off-grid moving up or down. I'm considering whether each 3 actually shifts to the far end of its local run of zeros relative to the 8, but that doesn't cleanly fit either. Let me instead check if this is really about row shifts rather than column shifts, comparing input row 1 against the output.

Testing whether the non-8 values in each row shift right by one position works for row 1 of the third query, matching the output exactly. Now checking row 2 with the same shift-right-by-one rule on its non-8 sequence.

But that puts the 3 at column 4, while the actual output shows it at column 1 - the rule doesn't hold consistently across rows. Trying shift left instead: row 0 works when shifted left, but row 2 doesn't match either, landing at column 2 instead of the observed column 1. Comparing more carefully, the 3 in row 2 moved left by two positions rather than one, while row 1's 3 moved right by two positions - so the shift amount seems to be 2, just in different directions per row.

Testing whether entire rows are simply reversed: row 4 reversed matches perfectly, but row 2 reversed fails because the 8 lands in the wrong spot even though the 3 lines up. Trying yet another angle, I'm tracking where each 3 starts and ends across all rows to see if there's a diagonal or vertical shift pattern instead - matching up input positions to output positions to spot a consistent movement rule.

That single-step theory fails too, so I'm re-deriving query2 by tracking each 3's column position: input has fives at (0,0),(1,4),(2,2),(3,0),(4,4), output shifts them to (1,1),(2,0),(3,2),(4,3), and I'm checking whether each moved one step toward or away from the 8 in its column.

I try a diagonal movement rule instead, testing whether each 3 shifts down-left by one cell, but the outputs don't line up with that pattern either.

Looking at the pairing between input and output positions, I suspect each 3 pairs with its nearest neighbor and shifts toward it by one step, like (0,0) moving down-right toward (1,1) and (3,0) moving up toward (2,0).

Trying training pair 1 again, both 3s at (1,4) and (2,4) shifted left by different amounts, so I'm reconsidering whether the movement depends on distance to some anchor point rather than a fixed direction.

Testing r2: does it exit or stay at col0? Output keeps 3 at (2,0), so maybe it only exits if it started already touching the wall. That fits r0. But r3 shows a new 3 appearing at col2 in the output row that shouldn't have one — I need to figure out where that extra 3 came from, maybe from wrapping or a different rule entirely.

For r4 [8,8,8,0,3], sliding left lands the 3 at col3, matching the output. For query3's r0 [3,0,0,0,8], the 3 at col0 wraps to col4 where the 8 blocks it, so it disappears — consistent. But r1 [0,3,8,0,0] sliding left should put the 3 at col0, yet the output shows it at col3, which contradicts a simple leftward slide — maybe the direction of movement isn't always left after all.

Testing wraparound: the 3 slides left through zeros, wraps from col0 to col4, then continues through zeros until blocked by the 8 at col2, stopping at col3 — that matches r1's output exactly. Checking r2 [0,0,3,0,0] with the same wraparound logic: since the row is all zeros with no 8 to block it, the 3 would cycle indefinitely, yet the output places it back at col0.

For query2 r0 [3,0,0,8,8], the 3 is immediately blocked when it wraps into the 8 at col4, so instead of staying put it seems to vanish entirely from the output — while in r2's all-zero case it lands at col0. So maybe the rule is: if immediately blocked with no movement possible, the piece disappears, but if it can move freely with no blocker, it still resolves to col0 for some reason I need to figure out.

Testing this against query3: row [8,0,0,3,0] sliding the 3 left hits the 8 at col0, stopping one space short at col1 — matches. Row [3,8,8,8,8] has the 3 immediately blocked wrapping around to the 8s, so it vanishes — matches too. Row [0,0,0,0,3] has no 8s to block against, so there's no landing rule to test there.

The rule I'm settling on: the marker slides leftward with wraparound until an 8 blocks it, stopping one cell before the block; if it can't move at all it vanishes; with no 8s in the row it just goes to col0. This checks out against the query2 and training examples too, including rows where the marker is immediately blocked and vanishes.

Now I'm applying this to the actual test grid, an 8x7 layout, starting with the first row which has two 3s that I'll need to handle separately.

I'm considering whether the leading 3 vanishes on contact with the 8 while the trailing 3 shifts left into its spot, or whether the whole block stays frozen since it can't move as a unit. The prior examples of vanishing all involved single 3s blocked immediately, so I need to figure out if that rule extends to adjacent pairs.

Working through row3: the block slides left until hitting the 8 at col3, landing the 3s at cols4-5. Rows4-6 have no 3s so they stay unchanged. I notice only the first four rows contain 3s, suggesting the shape might actually be a 4x2 block sliding leftward as a unit rather than per-row independently.

Considering it as a single 2D object across rows0-3, cols6-7, it can't slide left since row0's col5 is already blocked by an 8 — so the whole block would just stay put rather than vanish. I think treating each row's slide independently and letting blocked segments simply stop in place is the safer, more consistent rule, so I'll stick with my per-row answer.

This is consistent with wrapping around and exiting only when immediately blocked at the edge, so a 3 blocked mid-row simply stays put. I'll go with that interpretation.
